q: By what mechanism does spinal cord stimulation relieve pain?
o: Stimulating large A-beta fibres in the dorsal columns, activating inhibitory interneurons (gate control)
why: Dorsal column stimulation activates A-beta fibres and inhibitory interneurons that "gate" pain.

q: Which is an indication for a spinal cord stimulator?
o: Failed back surgery syndrome or CRPS
why: Indications include FBSS, CRPS type 1, refractory neuropathic pain, ischaemic pain and refractory angina.

q: Why is the trial lead often placed under local anaesthetic with light sedation?
o: So the patient can report where the paraesthesia is felt
why: Over-sedation stops the patient reporting paraesthesia coverage.

q: What is needed before permanent implantation of a stimulator?
o: A successful trial (typically over 50% pain reduction) and psychological assessment
why: Selection: pain over 6 months, refractory, definite diagnosis, successful trial and psychological assessment.

q: Where is the pulse generator usually placed?
o: In the gluteal region or anterior abdominal wall
why: Usually in the buttock or abdominal wall; leads are often around T8–10.

q: What is the commonest delayed complication of spinal cord stimulators?
why: Lead migration or fracture, infection and device failure are common delayed problems.

q: How can migraine aura be distinguished from a TIA?
o: Aura spreads gradually and sequentially; TIA symptoms start suddenly and together
why: TIA symptoms are typically sudden and simultaneous; migraine aura spreads gradually.

q: Which drug is used to prevent frequent migraine?
why: Preventives include propranolol, topiramate and valproate; triptans treat attacks.
